name: Interview brainteasers, set 3
description: Brainteasers of the kind interviewers ask: hats, weighings, backward induction, schedules, divisibility, doubling, sums, handshakes, trains and cubes. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Six prisoners, numbered 0 to 5, wear hats numbered 0 to 5, and numbers may repeat. Each sees the other five hats but not their own. All write a guess at once, with no signals, after agreeing a plan.
items.question: Which plan makes sure at least one prisoner guesses right?

options.text: Prisoner k guesses the number that makes all six hats total k, modulo 6.
Everyone guesses the number that makes the total 0, modulo 6.
options.why: You gave everyone the same target. When the total is not 0 modulo 6, all six are wrong.

options.text: Each guesses the number they see most often on the others.
options.why: You copied the crowd. With hats 0, 0, 1, 1, 2 and 2, everyone sees their own number least and guesses wrong.
You spread the guesses over hat numbers, not totals. Hats 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 0 on prisoners 0 to 5 make all six wrong.

feedback.correct: Correct. The six targets cover every possible total.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give each prisoner a different guess about the total, modulo 6.

explain.text: The total of the six hats, modulo 6, is one of 0 to 5. Prisoner k bets it is k and guesses the hat that makes it so. Exactly one prisoner holds the true remainder, so exactly one is right every time.

items.prose: Eight coins look alike, but one is lighter than the rest. You have a balance with two pans.
items.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the light coin, and what is the first weighing?

options.why: You halved. A balance has three outcomes, so split the coins into three groups.
After 4 against 4, four suspects remain. One weighing settles at most three, so this needs 3.
The split is right, but you miscounted. Each outcome leaves at most 3 coins, settled in one more weighing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A weighing has three outcomes, so make each outcome leave at most three coins.

explain.text: Weigh 3 against 3: a rising pan holds the light coin, and level means it is among the 2 aside. One more weighing finds it among 3 or 2. A single weighing has only 3 outcomes for 8 cases, so 2 is the fewest.

items.prose: A pot starts at £4. Ann moves in rounds 1 and 3, Ben in round 2. The mover may take 3/4 of the pot, leaving 1/4 to the other, and the game ends. Or the mover passes and the pot doubles. If Ann passes in round 3, the £16 pot is shared equally.
items.question: Each plays for their own money. What does Ann do in round 1?

options.text: Pass, planning to take £12 in round 3
options.why: You assumed Ben passes in round 2. He takes £6 there rather than end with £4.

options.text: Pass in every round to share £16, £8 each
options.why: Sharing needs Ann to pass in round 3, but there she takes £12 rather than £8.

options.text: Pass, since the pot doubles to £8
options.why: A bigger pot helps only if Ben passes it on. He takes £6, leaving Ann £2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start in round 3 and work back one round at a time.

explain.text: In round 3 Ann takes £12 rather than share for £8. So in round 2 Ben takes £6 rather than pass and get £4. So in round 1 Ann takes £3 rather than pass and get £2.

items.prose: Four jobs take 3, 5, 2 and 6 hours. Two identical machines run at once, each doing one job at a time. A job cannot be split.
items.question: What is the smallest time, in hours, by which all four jobs can finish?

widget.accept: 8 hours: 6 + 2 on one machine, 5 + 3 on the other.
widget.label: Hours

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the 16 hours of work as evenly as you can between the machines.

byKey.serial: You ran the jobs one after another. Two machines can share the 16 hours.
byKey.in-order: You gave each job, in the listed order, to the freer machine. The 6-hour job came last and landed on a busy machine.
byKey.longest: Six hours is only the longest job. The other 10 hours of work cannot fit beside it in that time.

explain.text: The work totals 16 hours, so no plan finishes before 8. The split 6 + 2 and 5 + 3 reaches exactly 8 on each machine. A search of all 16 assignments confirms 8 is the best.

items.prose: You want a number that every whole number from 1 to 10 divides exactly.
items.question: What is the smallest such positive number?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the highest power of each prime up to 10.

byKey.factorial: You multiplied 1 to 10. That works but repeats factors, so keep only the highest power of each prime.
byKey.two-to-four: You kept $2^4 = 16$. Only $8 = 2^3$ is needed, so halve it.
byKey.two-squared: You kept only $2^2$. Then 8 does not divide it.

explain.text: The highest prime powers up to 10 are $2^3 = 8$, $3^2 = 9$, 5 and 7. Their product is $8 \times 9 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520$. A search upwards from 1 also stops first at 2,520.

items.prose: Weed on a pond doubles in area every day. Starting from one weed, it covers the pond on day 24.
items.question: Starting instead from 8 weeds, on which day is the pond covered?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many doublings turn 1 weed into 8.

byKey.divided: You divided 24 by 8. Growth is by doubling, so 8 weeds save 3 days, not a factor of 8.
byKey.subtracted: You took 8 days off. Eight weeds are only three doublings, so take off 3.

explain.text: One weed becomes 8 after 3 doublings. So 8 weeds run 3 days ahead of one weed. The pond is covered on day 24 − 3 = 21.

items.question: What is the sum? Give a decimal or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each term as $\tfrac1k - \tfrac1{k+1}$ and cancel neighbours.

byKey.from-one: You summed from k = 1. The terms start at k = 10, so the sum starts at 1/10.
byKey.first-only: You kept 1/10 but did not take off the last piece, 1/100.
byKey.from-whole: You took 1/10 from 1. The pieces run from 1/10 down to 1/100, so the sum is 1/10 − 1/100.

explain.text: Each term is $\tfrac1k - \tfrac1{k+1}$, so neighbours cancel. Only the first and last pieces survive: $\tfrac{1}{10} - \tfrac{1}{100}$. That is $\tfrac{9}{100} = 0.09$.

items.prose: Eleven people meet at a party. Some pairs shake hands, each pair at most once.
items.question: Can every one of the eleven shake an odd number of hands?

options.text: No. The counts sum to twice the handshakes, an even number, but eleven odd counts sum to an odd number.
Yes. Each person shakes exactly one hand.
options.why: That pairs everyone off, but eleven people leave one person over.
Then the counts sum to 55, an odd number. Each handshake adds 2 to the sum, so it must be even.

options.text: No. Nobody can shake all ten other hands.
options.why: Shaking ten hands is allowed. The block is the parity of the total.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the handshakes two ways: by person, and by pair.

explain.text: Each handshake adds 1 to two people's counts, so the counts sum to an even number. Eleven odd numbers sum to an odd number. So at least one person shakes an even number of hands.

items.prose: Two trains 90 miles apart head towards each other at 30 mph and 45 mph. A bird flies back and forth between them at 60 mph until they meet.
items.question: How far does the bird fly, in miles?

widget.accept: 72 miles: the trains meet after 90/75 = 1.2 hours.
widget.label: Miles

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find when the trains meet, then use the bird's speed.

byKey.slower-train: You timed the meeting by the slower train alone. The trains close at 30 + 45 = 75 mph.
byKey.difference: You used the gap between their speeds. Trains heading towards each other close at the sum, 75 mph.

explain.text: The trains close at 30 + 45 = 75 mph, so they meet after 90/75 = 1.2 hours. The bird flies the whole time at 60 mph. So it covers 60 × 1.2 = 72 miles, with no need to add up the zigzags.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first n cubes add to $\left(\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$.

byKey.squares: That is the sum of squares from the warm-up. The cubes add to the square of 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 20.
byKey.not-squared: You found 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 20 = 210. Square it for the cubes.

explain.text: The first n cubes add to the square of the first n whole numbers. Here $1 + 2 + \cdots + 20 = 210$. So the cubes add to $210^2 = 44{,}100$.
